title: Calm thought (96–99)
hookLine: calm is his thought, calm his word and deed; forests are delightful to the free

lines: A DARK ROOM, A PALM-LEAF FAN.
cards: In a story from the commentary, an elder monk is getting ready for bed in a dark room, with his young novice, a boy of about seven, helping him.
Fumbling in the dark, the old man swings a palm-leaf fan, and its tip accidentally strikes the boy in the eye. The boy is badly hurt. He doesn't cry out.

He covers the eye with one hand and keeps serving, bringing water with the other. Only when the elder notices the one hand and asks why does he learn what happened. And the boy's first words are to comfort his teacher.

teach.b: The commentary says the old monk was overcome and went to the Buddha, and the Buddha spoke verse ninety-six. In Müller's English: “His thought is quiet, quiet are his word and deed.” Calm thought, calm word, calm action.
We met the rule in the Dhammapada's very first verse: the mind comes first, manopubbangama, and what follows carries its quality. So a calm mind makes calm speech and calm deeds.
The boy had no panic to manage; the calm was already there.

Verse ninety-seven is a puzzle. In the Pali, its key words each carry two meanings. Read one way, it describes a terrible person: faithless, ungrateful, a house-breaker, someone who's thrown away every opportunity.
Read the other way, it describes the awakened one: beyond mere belief because they've seen for themselves, knowing the uncreated, having cut the links of rebirth, having left all hope of gain behind.
The verse seems to enjoy that double take, as if to say: don't judge by surface words.

teach.h: CALM IS CARRIED, NOT A PLACE.
teach.b: Verse ninety-eight says wherever such calm people live, village or forest, low ground or high, that place is delightful.
And verse ninety-nine: forests are delightful to the free, the very places where the pleasure-seeking crowd finds nothing to enjoy.
So calm isn't a place. It's carried. The boy carried it into a dark room.
The free carry it into the forest, and make the forest delightful.

how: Buddhist teachers use verse ninety-six to describe the fruit of practice as calm in thought, speech and action together, and forest monasteries are traditionally valued as places where that calm can grow.

o: a quiet mind that makes word and deed quiet
a mind emptied of every single thought
staying silent to avoid any argument

games.q: match the pieces of verses ninety-six to ninety-nine.

s: verse ninety-seven can be read as describing a terrible person or an awakened one
its key Pali words carry double meanings, a deliberate puzzle.
in the story, the novice cried out and blamed his teacher
he covered the eye, kept serving, and his first words comforted the old monk.
verse ninety-nine says forests are delightful to the free
where pleasure-seekers find nothing to enjoy.

games.q: you're a young novice. in the dark, your teacher's fan has struck your eye. he doesn't know. what did the boy in the story do?
o: cry out so he knows what he did.
cover the eye and keep serving, then comfort him.
games.why: he kept serving with one hand; when the elder found out, the boy's first words were to comfort him.

practice: Let the breath slow, and let the face soften, then the jaw, then the hands, until thought grows quieter.
Then think of one place you'll be today, the kitchen, the office, the car, a waiting room, and picture carrying this calm into it: calm thought first, then calm word, then calm deed.

wordCard.voice: Calm thought. When the mind is calm, word and deed follow calmly, and wherever the calm go, the place becomes delightful.

orig.note: Pali: calm, peaceful, from verse ninety-six: 'santam tassa manam hoti,' calm is his mind.

carryVoice: Your line: calm thought, calm word. The mind goes first, and the rest follows. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: His thought is quiet, quiet are his word and deed

sources.ref: Dhammapada 97–99; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of the novice of Tissa Thera of Kosambi (verse 96)
